title: Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Protocol for Schizosaccharomyces pombe
author: Khanduja, Motamedi

Carefully remove the supernatant from each tube into a pre-labeled new Eppendorf DNA LoBind tube.Note: Do not touch the interface while pipetting out the aqueous phase. We generally recover 450–460 μL of aqueous solution at this step.c.Add 450 μL of chloroform to each Eppendorf tube and mix by inverting the Eppendorf tubes at room temperature.d.Spin the Eppendorf tubes in a centrifuge at 13500 rpm for 12 min at room temperature. Carefully remove the supernatant from each Eppendorf tube into a pre-labeled new Eppendorf DNA LoBind tube.Note: Do not touch the interface while pipetting out the aqueous phase. We generally recover 380–400 μL of aqueous solution at this step.54.Ethanol Precipitation of ChIP DNA.a.Add 50 μL of 4 M LiCl solution and 960 μL of chilled 100% Ethanol to each Eppendorf tube. Mix the solutions by inverting the tubes multiple times and incubate them at −40°C for at least 2 h.Note: Alternatively, samples can be kept at −80°C for ethanol precipitation. Longer incubation periods at −80°C/−40°C for ethanol precipitation are also fine.Pause Point: The protocol can be paused at this point and samples can be stored at −80°C/−40°C.b.Take out the Eppendorf tubes from the −40°C freezer and spin them at 13500 rpm for 15 min at 4°C.c.Remove the supernatant with a P1000 micropipette, without disturbing the DNA pellet, and discard it.d.Add 500 μL of 70% Ethanol to each Eppendorf tube, gently tap them, and spin them at 13500 rpm for 15 min at 4°C.e.Remove the supernatant with a P200 micropipette, without disturbing the DNA pellet, and discard it.f.Dry the DNA pellets by keeping the Eppendorf tubes open in a tube rack at 37°C for 30 min.g.Resuspend the ChIP DNA pellets in 40 μL of 0.1x T.E. buffer and the Input DNA in 50 μL of 0.1x T.E. buffer. steps.title: Prepare yeast pre‑cultures
steps.instruction: Streak each S. pombe strain from –80 °C stocks onto YEA‑agar plates with the appropriate antibiotics, incubate at 32 °C for 2–3 days until isolated colonies appear; pick a single colony, inoculate into 7 mL liquid YEA, and grow at 32 °C on a roller drum for 12–16 h.

substeps.instruction: Streak on YEA‑agar + antibiotics, incubate 32 °C 2–3 days.
Inoculate 7 mL YEA with a single colony, incubate 32 °C 12–16 h on roller.

steps.title: Thaw and resuspend crosslinked cells
steps.instruction: Remove the double‑crosslinked cell pellets from the –80 °C freezer, thaw at room temperature for 5 min, keep on ice and add 500 µL freshly prepared ChIP buffer to each pellet (pellet weight should be 0.12–0.14 g). Vortex briefly to obtain a homogeneous suspension.

substeps.instruction: Thaw pellets 5 min at RT.
Add 500 µL ChIP buffer (pellet 0.12–0.14 g) on ice.
Vortex to resuspend completely.

steps.title: Bead‑beating cell lysis
steps.instruction: Add one “scoop” (0.5 mL PCR tube full) of cold glass beads to each tube, place tubes in a MagNA Lyser and bead‑beat at 6000 rpm for 30 s at 4 °C; keep tubes on ice for 3 min after each beat. Repeat the bead‑beat / ice cycle three additional times (total four cycles).

substeps.instruction: Add 0.5 mL cold glass beads (scoop) to each tube.
Bead‑beat 6000 rpm 30 s at 4 °C.
Ice 3 min, repeat 3 more times (4 cycles total).

steps.title: Collect lysate via needle filtration
steps.instruction: Using a BD #305145 needle, punch a hole at the bottom of each 1.5 mL tube containing the lysed cells and place the tube into a pre‑chilled 5 mL polypropylene tube on ice; spin the 5 mL tubes in an Eppendorf 5810R swing‑bucket rotor at 4000 rpm for 1 min at 4 °C. Discard the original 1.5 mL tubes with beads, gently pipette the lysate from the 5 mL tubes with a P1000, and transfer it to pre‑chilled 1.5 mL polystyrene tubes (Caplugs Evergreen #214‑3721‑010) on ice, then cap.

substeps.instruction: Punch hole in 1.5 mL tube with BD #305145 needle, place into chilled 5 mL tube on ice.
Centrifuge 5 mL tubes 4000 rpm 1 min at 4 °C.
Discard 1.5 mL tubes with beads.
Resuspend lysate in 5 mL tube with P1000.
Transfer lysate to chilled 1.5 mL polystyrene tubes, keep on ice.

steps.title: Phenol‑chloroform DNA extraction
steps.instruction: Perform sequential phenol‑chloroform‑isoamyl alcohol and chloroform extractions on each lysate tube.

substeps.instruction: Add 500 µL phenol‑chloroform‑isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1), invert repeatedly at room temperature.
Spin 13500 rpm 12 min at room temperature; transfer the aqueous phase (~450–460 µL) to a new LoBind tube, avoiding the interface.
Add 450 µL chloroform, invert at room temperature.
Spin 13500 rpm 12 min at room temperature; transfer the aqueous phase (~380–400 µL) to a new LoBind tube, avoiding the interface.

steps.title: Ethanol precipitation and DNA resuspension
steps.instruction: Precipitate DNA with LiCl/ethanol, wash, dry, and resuspend for downstream use.

substeps.instruction: Add 50 µL 4 M LiCl and 960 µL chilled 100 % ethanol, invert to mix, and incubate at –40 °C for ≥2 h (or at –80 °C).
Pause point: samples may be stored at –40 °C/–80 °C.
Spin 13500 rpm 15 min at 4 °C; discard supernatant without disturbing the pellet.
Add 500 µL 70 % ethanol, tap gently, spin 13500 rpm 15 min at 4 °C; discard supernatant.
Dry DNA pellets open at 37 °C for 30 min.
Resuspend ChIP DNA pellets in 40 µL 0.1× TE buffer (Input DNA in 50 µL 0.1× TE). Incubate 37 °C for 1 h on a thermomixer shaking at 1000 rpm.
Briefly spin in a micro‑fuge and store at –80 °C/–40 °C.

description: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) is a well-established technique that has enabled the mapping of histone tail modifications and the binding sites of chromatin-associated proteins at specific genomic loci or throughout the genome using ChIP followed by quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR) or ChIP followed by deep sequencing (ChIP-seq), respectively. These techniques provide quantitative information about the occurrence of a given histone mark or the localization of a chromatin-binding protein to a given DNA sequence (ChIP-qPCR) or DNA sequences throughout the genome (ChIP-seq). The ChIP assay involves four steps: (1) crosslinking of chromatin-binding proteins to DNA, (2) chromatin fragmentation, (3) immunoprecipitation of target protein using a high-specificity antibody, and (4) identification and quantification of immunoprecipitated DNA using qPCR or next-generation sequencing. Apart from the antibody specificity, the success of a ChIP assay depends on the efficient crosslinking of proteins of interest to DNA. A single crosslink approach using formaldehyde, which crosslinks proteins with DNA within its short spacer arm length of 2Å, has been useful in mapping the binding sites of proteins that directly bind to DNA such as transcription factors, histones, and its post-translational modifications. However, formaldehyde inefficiently crosslinks chromatin-binding proteins which do not interact with DNA directly, such as transcriptional coactivators and corepressors, chromatin regulators, and proteins that transiently interact with chromatin. These complexes often interact with DNA indirectly and are recruited to chromatin as a part of multi-subunit complexes by binding to a histone modification, and/or interacting with a DNA- or RNA-binding protein.
